Nonetheless, the data collected provided a robust basis for evaluating the primary 426 diagnostic performance objectives. Second, according to the protocol, the reference standard 427 comprised DAT, PCR on DBS specimens, or microscopy where available; however, no 428 microscopy was performed due to facility constraints, and all PCR assays on DBS were 429 negative, due to low DNA yields from the DBS. Consequently, analyses relied primarily on 430 DAT as the reference, which may introduce misclassification bias owing to its imperfect 431 sensitivity and specificity compared to parasitological or molecular confirmation. 432

text.text: Leishmania infantum and L. donovani and transmitted by a bite of an infected female phlebotomine sandfly.

The disease disproportionately affects impoverished and underserved populations, where inadequate access to healthcare contributes to delayed diagnosis, treatment, and increased morbidity and mortality.
In Kenya, 11 out of the 47 counties are known to be endemic for VL.
Visceral Leishmaniasis is fatal if it's not timely diagnosed and treated.
Parasitological methods remain the gold standard for diagnosing and confirming VL, but they are invasive and require specialised training and equipment.

Serological tests in the form of Rapid Diagnostic Tests (RDTs) are widely used for initial screening and detection but can still report positive results for long periods after curative treatment due to the persistence of anti-VL antibodies.
It is recommended that VL diagnosis follows an algorithmic approach.
This study evaluated the diagnostic performance of rK28 and rK39 RDTs (Kala-azar Detect and IT Leish) in various algorithmic combinations against a composite reference standard in Kenya.
We evaluated rK28 and Kala-azar Detect along with rK39 IT-Leish as index tests, and Direct Agglutination Test (DAT) as the reference standard test.
Participants were recruited from seven health facilities located in VL endemic regions of Marsabit and Turkana counties, Kenya.
Blood samples were collected, as well as patient demographic data.
Treatment decisions followed the national diagnostic algorithm and health facility routine procedures.
Diagnostic test performance was assessed individually, in parallel, and based on sequential algorithmic combinations.
Specificity, sensitivity, balanced accuracy, and negative and positive predictive values were statistically estimated.
Results: A total of 398 participants were recruited for the study, with fever and splenomegaly being the most reported clinical symptoms.
Individually, the rK28 kit demonstrated a sensitivity of 96%, a specificity of 86%, and a balanced accuracy (BA) of 91.2%.

Visceral leishmaniasis (VL), or kala-azar, is a severe and potentially fatal disease caused by Leishmania parasites (1).

text.text: Although around 20 species of Leishmania parasites cause leishmaniasis, only two (Leishmania infantum and L. donovani) are attributed to causing VL (2, 3).

text.text: The parasites are zoonotic and are transmitted by female phlebotomine sandflies during feeding(4).

Visceral Leishmaniasis is estimated to have a global incidence rate of approximately 500,000 cases annually, resulting in approximately 50,000 deaths, with between 200 million and 400 million people at risk of contracting the disease (1, 5).

text.text: This study evaluated the diagnostic performance of rK28, rK39 IT-Leish, and rK39 Kala-azar Detect, individually and in algorithmic combinations, using DAT as the reference standard.
The study was conducted across seven sentinel sites in northern Kenya.
The study provides essential evidence to inform national diagnostic policy, optimise RDT deployment across health system levels, and support ongoing VL elimination efforts.
This was a single-arm, non-interventional, prospective diagnostic accuracy study evaluating the performance of rK28, Kala-azar Detect, and IT-Leish RDTs, individually and in algorithmic combinations.
The originally pre-specified composite reference standard included DAT, PCR, and microscopy where available.

Participants were consecutively enrolled as they presented to seven health facilities in Marsabit (Laisamis, Marsabit and Moyale) and Turkana (Lopiding, Kakuma, Lodwar and Namoruputh) counties in northern Kenya (Fig 1) between January 2023 and March 2024.

text.text: The study sites included health centres, sub-county hospitals, and county referral hospitals selected based on VL burden and diagnostic capacity 33 .
Eligible participants were individuals aged ≥1 year presenting with clinical signs and symptoms suggestive of VL, including fever of more than two weeks, splenomegaly, and weight loss.
Individuals who tested negative for malaria and were considered VL suspects according to national guidelines were also eligible for participation.
Written informed consent was obtained from all adult participants and from parents or legal guardians for minors, with assent obtained from children aged 12-17 years where applicable.

Individuals with VL relapses within the previous 6-12 months, post-kalaazar dermal leishmaniasis (PKDL), or inability to provide the required 2ml of blood were excluded. of health facilities where the study was conducted.
Demographic and clinical data were collected and recorded from all patients who visited the treatment facilities and consented to participate in the study.
The participants were tested using rK39 IT-Leish, rK28, and rK39 Kala-azar Detect, according to the manufacturers' instructions.
In line with national guidelines, rK39 IT-Leish was performed first, followed by rK28 and Kala-azar Detect.
All tests were performed and interpreted by trained laboratory personnel using standardised operating procedures.
Clinical management followed the national diagnostic guidelines (IT-Leish rK39 followed by DAT for case confirmation), ensuring that the results of study RDTs did not influence patient care (Fig 2).

This study evaluated the diagnostic accuracy and operational characteristics of rK28 and rK39based RDTs, as well as multiple algorithmic diagnostic approaches, for VL diagnosis in East Africa.

Additionally, the study also investigated sociodemographic factors that may influence health-seeking behaviors, specifically looking at delays in going to the health facility and incurred diagnostic costs.
The findings provide critical context to regional diagnostic needs amidst ongoing changes in test availability and programmatic priorities.

text.text: While ideal for initial screening, these tests require confirmatory diagnosis or clinical verification to reduce overtreatment risks.
Operational advantages of rK28 include stability at high temperatures and a 24-month shelf life, addressing common challenges in storage and distribution.
The frequent IT-Leish rK39 stockouts observed in this study further underscore the value of alternative platforms like rK28.
However, its clinical adoption remains limited due to its research-use-only status, pending additional evidence, regulatory approval, and inclusion in national diagnostic guidelines.

The IT-Leish rK39 test, recommended by the WHO for VL diagnosis and incorporated into Kenya's national diagnostic algorithm, demonstrated high specificity of 93.4% but comparatively lower sensitivity 87.4%.

These findings align with earlier studies done by Mbui et al that reported similar low sensitivity in Kenya 89.3%(39) and regional meta-analyses by Cunningham et al, which reported a pooled sensitivity of 85.1% and specificity of 96.0% (40).

text.text: Kala-azar Detect rK39 provides a high specificity of 91.1% and moderate positive predictive value of 86.6%, making it a reliable tool for ruling in VL, although a low sensitivity of 67.4% was observed in this study.

This low sensitivity is consistent with findings from Ethiopia and Sudan (38, 41), and its moderate diagnostic performance (balanced accuracy 79.3%), limit its suitability for elimination-focused programs.

text.text: Where drug toxicity remains a concern, positives-retested algorithms (e.g., rK28→rK39 Kala-azar Detect) may be used for confirmatory testing, offering higher specificity (94.1%) but lower sensitivity (65.1%).

However, the improved safety profile of newer VL treatments like miltefosine(47), reduces the risks of overtreatment, supporting the use of high-sensitivity diagnostic algorithms to minimize missed cases and advance elimination efforts.
Double-test algorithms can enhance diagnostic accuracy for VL and support elimination goals in East Africa but involve higher costs, logistical complexity, and greater demands on health systems.
Their success depends on formal inclusion in national guidelines, flexible policies, and strong support systems, including training, supply chains, and health information infrastructure.
However, with coordinated planning, these strategies can turn improved accuracy into real progress toward VL elimination.
The findings of this study show that rK28 has a higher sensitivity and balanced accuracy compared to the rK39-based RDTs evaluated.

These results suggest rK28 is particularly suitable in elimination settings for use in peripheral health facilities, where missing true VL cases have important clinical and epidemiological implications.

The observed performance differences between rK28 and the Kala-azar Detect rK39 test are consistent with previous reports highlighting variability in the performance of rK39-based assays in East African settings (48).

text.text: The results align with previous evaluations conducted in Ethiopia, Sudan, and South Sudan, which have consistently demonstrated improved diagnostic performance of rK28 compared with rK39-based tests.
The consistently high sensitivity of rK28 across regions suggests that it may be less affected by antigenic variability among circulating L. donovani strains.
In contrast, the variable performance of rK39-based tests in East Africa may reflect both parasite diversity and host immunological factors.
Parallel testing algorithms further improved sensitivity, approaching near-complete case detection.
This is particularly relevant for VL elimination efforts, where undiagnosed cases contribute to ongoing transmission.
However, increased sensitivity comes with reduced specificity, which could lead to overtreatment in some contexts.
Series testing approaches increased specificity, making them more suitable for confirmatory purposes or settings where overtreatment poses significant clinical or programmatic risks.
Collectively, the findings highlight the need for diagnostic strategies that are both highperforming and contextually feasible, particularly for underserved or high-risk populations.

While the study achieved valuable insights into VL diagnostics, enrolment did not reach the 423 initially planned sample size, which resulted in insufficient statistical power to perform 424 secondary analyses such as cost-effectiveness assessment and evaluation of optimal test 425 placement.
Nonetheless, the data collected provided a robust basis for evaluating the primary 426 diagnostic performance objectives.

Second, according to the protocol, the reference standard 427 comprised DAT, PCR on DBS specimens, or microscopy where available; however, no 428 microscopy was performed due to facility constraints, and all PCR assays on DBS were 429 negative, due to low DNA yields from the DBS.

Consequently, analyses relied primarily on 430 DAT as the reference, which may introduce misclassification bias owing to its imperfect 431 sensitivity and specificity compared to parasitological or molecular confirmation.
Algorithmic testing strategies and platforms such as rK28 present substantial opportunities to strengthen VL diagnostics and support elimination objectives in East Africa.

However, the durable impact will depend on their adoption as clinical-use tests (rK28), incorporation into policy and national guidelines, and the underpinning of resilient supply chains and health systems.

Optimisation of diagnostic strategies tailored to local capacity, epidemiology, and programmatic aims will be essential for maximizing accuracy, limiting overtreatment, and advancing regional VL elimination objectives.
Continued operational evaluation remains critical to fully realise the potential of available RDTs in the evolving landscape.

Notably, building on the diagnostic accuracy data presented, further research on the cost-effectiveness analyses is recommended to guide practical implementation and ensure efficient, sustainable progress toward VL elimination targets.
Given the discontinuation of IT-Leish and the lower performance of Kala-azar Detect rK39, Kenya's national diagnostic algorithm should be revised to integrate rK28 as the primary diagnostic tool.

Strengthening supply chains, ensuring wide availability of high-performing RDTs, and building capacity for their effective use will be essential for achieving national and regional VL elimination targets.
